descriptors.concept_name: Factors to be Considered When Investigating Variance
descriptors.definition: Organizations assess specific elements such as variance size, cost-benefit trade-offs, and temporal patterns before deciding to investigate performance differences. If budgets prove unrealistic, management should re-evaluate the budgeting process rather than review individual variances.
inclusion: evaluating cost versus benefit of investigations
assessing variance magnitude and worsening trends
re-evaluating uncontrollable budgets
nearby_distinctions: Differs from variance computation methods by focusing on the operational and economic decision criteria governing whether to pursue an investigation.

descriptors.definition: Management evaluates operational discrepancies using structured decision frameworks such as arbitrary rule of thumb criteria or statistical probability models. These approaches help determine whether a cost system is operating normally or requires formal intervention.
instrument_references: Management and Cost Accounting by Colin M. Drury
inclusion: applying percentage or absolute threshold criteria
using statistical probability distributions to flag operational deviations
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts with variance interpretation which identifies qualitative root causes rather than the mathematical or decision thresholds triggering an investigation.

descriptors.definition: This model relies on managerial judgment and arbitrary criteria to decide whether cost variances warrant investigation. Triggers include absolute variance sizes exceeding monetary limits or variance-to-cost ratios surpassing predetermined percentages.
instrument_references: Management and Cost Accounting by Colin M. Drury
inclusion: investigating absolute variance amounts over a fixed threshold
assessing variances exceeding specified cost ratios
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from statistical decision models by its reliance on subjective managerial rules rather than probability distributions of in-control systems.

descriptors.definition: This approach evaluates variances by assuming two mutually exclusive states where a system is either in control with random fluctuations or out of control. Investigations are triggered when the statistical probability of an observation coming from an in-control distribution falls below a chosen level.
instrument_references: Management and Cost Accounting by Colin M. Drury
inclusion: evaluating observations against in-control distributions
initiating corrective action based on statistical probability triggers
nearby_distinctions: Unlike the simple rule of thumb model, this approach uses formal probability thresholds to distinguish random fluctuations from systemic process failures.

descriptors.definition: Interdependence describes how the underlying cause of one variance can partially or wholly explain another, requiring simultaneous evaluation of multiple variances. For instance, purchasing cheaper, lower-quality material may create a favorable material price variance while simultaneously causing an adverse material usage variance due to increased wastage.
instrument_references: Management and Cost Accounting by Colin M. Drury
inclusion: analyzing correlated cost variances together
linking material quality trade-offs to usage impacts
evaluating trade-offs between labour rate and productivity
exclusion: analyzing standard cost variances completely in isolation
treating operational variances as independent events
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from single variance interpretation by emphasizing the interactive cause-and-effect relationships linking multiple operational variances.

descriptors.definition: This variance reflects differences in material acquisition costs caused by supplier changes, order sizes, or purchasing inefficiencies. Additional drivers include unexpected delivery charge increases and emergency purchases necessitated by poor inventory control.
inclusion: identifying supplier-related cost changes
evaluating purchasing procedure inefficiencies
assessing emergency purchase cost impacts
nearby_distinctions: Unlike material usage variance which measures physical quantities consumed, material price variance focuses strictly on acquisition costs and purchasing conditions.

descriptors.definition: This variance captures discrepancies in the physical quantity of materials consumed compared to standard expectations. Potential causes include purchasing inferior materials, changing production designs, handling carelessness, material pilferage, and poor quality inspection.
inclusion: tracking production wastage rates
identifying material handling and pilferage issues
evaluating quality control and design impacts
nearby_distinctions: Differs from material price variance by focusing on physical consumption quantities and wastage rather than purchasing rates and supplier pricing.

descriptors.definition: This variance measures unexpected deviations in direct payroll expenses arising from pay rate changes or workforce structure adjustments. Key drivers include wage rate increases, bonus payments, and shifts in workforce composition or experience levels.
inclusion: tracking unexpected wage rate increases
evaluating workforce composition changes
accounting for direct labour bonus payments
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts with labour efficiency variance, which measures time utilization and productivity rather than hourly wage rate fluctuations.

descriptors.definition: This variance reflects productivity differences driven by workforce performance, supervision quality, and operational disruptions. Potential triggers include learning curve effects, resource shortages, inferior material inputs, and machinery introductions.
inclusion: evaluating learning curve productivity impacts
assessing supervision and industrial action effects
analyzing resource shortage delays
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from labour rate variance by measuring time and productivity performance rather than hourly wage compensation differentials.

descriptors.definition: Overhead variances encompass discrepancies in fixed and variable manufacturing overheads resulting from spending levels or volume fluctuations. Fixed expenditure variances arise from excess spending, while variable expenditure variances typically stem from machine running cost changes.
inclusion: analyzing excess fixed overhead budget spending
evaluating fixed overhead volume changes
tracking variable overhead machine cost shifts
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from direct cost variances by evaluating indirect manufacturing costs categorized into fixed and variable expenditure and volume components.

descriptors.definition: This variance measures the impact of actual selling price deviations compared to budgeted prices across products. Causes include customer discounts for bulk purchases, promotional marketing offers, sales personnel performance, and broad industry economic conditions.
inclusion: evaluating customer bulk purchase discounts
assessing pricing impacts of marketing campaigns
tracking industry-wide economic price shifts
nearby_distinctions: Contrasts with sales volume variance by focusing strictly on unit selling price realizations rather than quantities sold.

descriptors.definition: This variance tracks the financial effect of selling a different total quantity of goods than budgeted. Underlying causes include direct selling and marketing effectiveness, customer preference shifts, production difficulties satisfying demand, and price elasticity effects.
inclusion: evaluating sales mix and quantity contribution effects
assessing marketing and direct selling performance
analyzing demand changes from pricing adjustments
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from sales price variance by measuring volume and mix performance rather than unit price deviations.
